subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is atrophy?

options.text: Decrease in cell size and tissue mass

rationales.whyCorrect: Atrophy reduces organ size through smaller cells and sometimes cell loss.
rationales.eli10: Cells shrink when less work or support is available.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is hypertrophy?

options.text: Change to another mature cell type

rationales.whyCorrect: Hypertrophy enlarges existing cells without necessarily adding cells.
rationales.eli10: Each worker grows bigger instead of hiring more workers.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is hyperplasia?

rationales.whyCorrect: Hyperplasia enlarges tissue by increasing the population of cells.
rationales.eli10: The tissue gets bigger by adding more cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is dysplasia?

rationales.whyCorrect: Dysplasia features abnormal size, shape, and organization and may be precancerous.
rationales.eli10: Cells grow in a messy, unusual pattern.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What distinguishes apoptosis?

options.text: It affects large tissue areas randomly

rationales.whyCorrect: Apoptosis removes individual cells through an organized, energy-dependent process.
rationales.eli10: A damaged cell follows a tidy self-removal plan.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What characterizes necrosis?

options.text: Uncontrolled cell injury with membrane rupture

rationales.whyCorrect: Necrotic cells swell, lose membrane integrity, and provoke inflammation.
rationales.eli10: The cell breaks open messily and alarms nearby tissue.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which finding commonly indicates reversible cell injury?

rationales.whyCorrect: ATP depletion initially disrupts ion pumps, allowing sodium and water to accumulate.
rationales.eli10: A tired cell cannot pump salt out, so water makes it swell.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which is a common cause of cellular injury?

rationales.whyCorrect: Reduced blood flow deprives cells of oxygen and nutrients and impairs waste removal.
rationales.eli10: A blocked supply road starves the cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is metaplasia?

options.text: Reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another

rationales.whyCorrect: Metaplasia adapts tissue by substituting a more stress-resistant mature cell type.
rationales.eli10: The tissue swaps one trained worker type for another.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A skeletal muscle shrinks after weeks in a cast. Which adaptation occurred?

rationales.whyCorrect: Reduced workload lowers protein synthesis and muscle-cell size.
rationales.eli10: Unused muscle fibers become smaller.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Heart muscle thickens after long-standing pressure overload. What is this?

rationales.whyCorrect: Cardiac muscle cells enlarge to generate more force against resistance.
rationales.eli10: Each heart cell grows bigger to push against extra pressure.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Hormonal stimulation increases gland-cell number. Which process is occurring?

rationales.whyCorrect: Hormone-responsive cells can divide, increasing tissue mass.
rationales.eli10: The signal tells the gland to add more cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Blood flow returns quickly after brief ischemia, and cells recover. How is the injury classified?

rationales.whyCorrect: Prompt restoration before critical membrane and mitochondrial damage permits recovery.
rationales.eli10: The supply arrived before the cell passed the point of no return.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which finding most strongly indicates irreversible injury?

options.text: Severe membrane damage with enzyme leakage

rationales.whyCorrect: Loss of membrane integrity marks inability to restore cellular homeostasis.
rationales.eli10: Once the cell's walls break badly, normal balance cannot return.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A tissue loses cells without nearby inflammation. Which mechanism is likely?

rationales.whyCorrect: Apoptotic fragments are rapidly cleared without spilling inflammatory contents.
rationales.eli10: The cell packages itself neatly, so no messy alarm spreads.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Brain tissue becomes liquid after infarction. Which necrosis pattern is typical?

rationales.whyCorrect: Enzymatic digestion commonly produces liquefactive necrosis in the brain.
rationales.eli10: Damaged brain tissue is digested into a soft liquid area.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Smoking causes airway columnar cells to become squamous cells. What is this?

rationales.whyCorrect: Chronic irritation drives replacement with a tougher mature cell type.
rationales.eli10: The airway trades delicate cells for tougher ones.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does hypoxia first impair sodium-potassium pumps?

rationales.whyCorrect: Oxidative phosphorylation declines, leaving insufficient ATP for membrane pumps.
rationales.eli10: Low oxygen means fewer energy coins to run the salt pump.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A chemical generates free radicals. What cellular target may be damaged?

rationales.whyCorrect: Reactive oxygen species oxidize multiple cellular components.
rationales.eli10: Chemical sparks can scorch walls, machines, and instructions.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Calcium floods an injured cell. Why is this harmful?

rationales.whyCorrect: Excess cytosolic calcium activates proteases, phospholipases, and endonucleases.
rationales.eli10: Too much calcium switches on scissors that cut cell parts.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A liver enlarges because remaining cells divide after partial removal. What is this?

rationales.whyCorrect: Regenerative signals stimulate capable cells to replace lost tissue mass.
rationales.eli10: The remaining liver cells make more teammates.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which response helps an injured cell manage misfolded proteins?

rationales.whyCorrect: Protective responses slow translation and increase chaperones or degradation.
rationales.eli10: The cell pauses the factory and sends helpers to refold mistakes.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A cell's nucleus fragments into dense pieces. What is this called?

rationales.whyCorrect: Karyorrhexis is fragmentation of a condensed, dying nucleus.
rationales.eli10: The damaged DNA room breaks into dark pieces.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does ischemia usually injure tissue faster than isolated hypoxia?

options.text: It also removes nutrients and impairs waste clearance

rationales.whyCorrect: Ischemia limits oxygen and substrates while allowing metabolites to accumulate.
rationales.eli10: The road closure blocks supplies and trash pickup together.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How can reperfusion worsen ischemic injury?

options.text: Sudden oxygen can generate reactive species and inflammation

rationales.whyCorrect: Restored flow can produce oxidative stress and recruit inflammatory injury despite being necessary.
rationales.eli10: Restarting flow can create a burst of damaging sparks.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can dysplasia be reversible yet clinically important?

options.text: Removing the stress may restore order, but persistent dysplasia may progress
It is identical to normal growth

rationales.whyCorrect: Early disordered growth may regress, whereas ongoing genetic injury raises neoplastic risk.
rationales.eli10: The messy pattern can improve, but repeated damage may make it worse.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which sequence best describes worsening hypoxic injury?

options.text: ATP loss, pump failure, swelling, membrane damage

rationales.whyCorrect: Energy failure causes ionic imbalance and swelling before critical structural failure.
rationales.eli10: First power fails, then pumps stop, the cell swells, and walls break.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does coagulative necrosis preserve tissue outlines temporarily?

rationales.whyCorrect: Denatured structural proteins and enzymes delay breakdown of dead cells.
rationales.eli10: Heat-like damage stiffens the tissue before cleanup removes it.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A tissue adapts to stress but becomes less specialized. What tradeoff occurred?

options.text: Greater resistance at the cost of normal function

rationales.whyCorrect: Metaplastic cells may tolerate stress better while performing the original role less well.
rationales.eli10: Tougher replacement workers may not do the old job as skillfully.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is mitochondrial permeability a pivotal injury event?

options.text: It collapses energy production and can release death signals

rationales.whyCorrect: Damaged mitochondria lose membrane potential and release apoptosis-promoting proteins.
rationales.eli10: When the power plants fail, energy stops and self-destruct messages escape.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which cell commonly arrives early in acute bacterial inflammation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Neutrophils rapidly leave blood to phagocytose microbes and debris.
rationales.eli10: These fast defender cells reach the problem first.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which cell is prominent in chronic inflammation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Macrophages sustain inflammation, clear debris, and direct repair.
rationales.eli10: These long-working cleanup cells also send many signals.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What causes redness in acute inflammation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Widened arterioles increase local blood flow.
rationales.eli10: More blood makes the injured area look red.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which mediator is released by mast cells and increases vascular permeability?

rationales.whyCorrect: Histamine rapidly dilates vessels and opens endothelial gaps.
rationales.eli10: Histamine makes tiny vessels wider and leakier.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is chemotaxis?

options.text: Directed cell movement along a chemical gradient

rationales.whyCorrect: Leukocytes follow increasing concentrations of chemoattractants toward injury.
rationales.eli10: Defender cells follow a chemical trail.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is regeneration?

options.text: Replacement with the same functional cell type

rationales.whyCorrect: Regeneration restores injured tissue using surviving cells or stem cells.
rationales.eli10: The body replaces broken workers with the same kind.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which cell produces collagen during scar formation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Fibroblasts synthesize collagen and extracellular matrix.
rationales.eli10: Fibroblasts are repair workers that lay strong fibers.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is granulation tissue?

options.text: New capillaries and fibroblasts in healing tissue

rationales.whyCorrect: Granulation tissue is vascular repair tissue that fills a wound.
rationales.eli10: It is pink new repair material full of tiny vessels and builders.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which is a classic sign of inflammation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Fluid leakage and cellular entry produce swelling.
rationales.eli10: Extra fluid and helpers make the area puffy.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A sprained ankle swells within hours. What explains the edema?

rationales.whyCorrect: Endothelial gaps let protein-rich fluid move into tissue.
rationales.eli10: Leaky vessels let fluid collect around the injury.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Leukocytes roll along vessel walls before exiting. Which molecules mediate rolling?

rationales.whyCorrect: Selectins form weak transient bonds that slow leukocytes.
rationales.eli10: Small sticky contacts make defender cells roll instead of race past.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A wound contains pus. What largely forms it?

rationales.whyCorrect: Purulent exudate contains accumulated neutrophils and breakdown material.
rationales.eli10: Pus is a pile of defenders, germs, and damaged pieces.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does inflamed tissue hurt?

options.text: Mediators sensitize nerves and swelling adds pressure

rationales.whyCorrect: Bradykinin, prostaglandins, and tissue pressure activate pain pathways.
rationales.eli10: Alarm chemicals and puffiness press the area's pain buttons.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A clean incision has closely opposed edges. How will it mainly heal?

rationales.whyCorrect: Primary-intention healing uses little granulation tissue and leaves a smaller scar.
rationales.eli10: Edges placed together need only a narrow bridge.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A large open wound closes from its base and edges. Which pattern fits?

rationales.whyCorrect: Secondary intention involves abundant granulation tissue, contraction, and a larger scar.
rationales.eli10: A wide gap needs more filling and pulling together.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A foreign body persists for months. Which response is likely?

rationales.whyCorrect: Persistent agents recruit macrophages, lymphocytes, and fibrosis.
rationales.eli10: When the problem stays, long-term crews keep working around it.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does poor perfusion delay wound healing?

options.text: It limits oxygen and nutrients needed for repair

rationales.whyCorrect: Repairing cells require blood-delivered oxygen, substrates, and immune support.
rationales.eli10: Builders cannot work well when supply trucks cannot arrive.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A corticosteroid reduces inflammation. Which consequence may follow?

rationales.whyCorrect: Suppressing mediators and leukocytes can also impair host defense and healing.
rationales.eli10: Turning down the alarm can also slow defenders and builders.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A fever follows release of inflammatory cytokines. What changes?

rationales.whyCorrect: Pyrogenic cytokines promote prostaglandins that raise the hypothalamic set point.
rationales.eli10: The brain's thermostat is temporarily turned higher.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A wound separates after sutures are removed too early. What failed?

rationales.whyCorrect: Early wounds have weak collagen and gain strength gradually.
rationales.eli10: The new fiber bridge was not strong enough yet.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which action of macrophages supports healing?

options.text: Clearing debris and releasing growth factors

rationales.whyCorrect: Macrophages transition the wound from cleanup toward rebuilding.
rationales.eli10: Cleanup cells also tell builders when to start.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A granuloma forms around a hard-to-eradicate pathogen. What cells organize it?

rationales.whyCorrect: Granulomas wall off persistent agents through coordinated cell-mediated immunity.
rationales.eli10: Defenders build a living fence around a stubborn problem.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does vitamin C deficiency impair healing?

options.text: Collagen synthesis and cross-linking are impaired

rationales.whyCorrect: Vitamin C supports hydroxylation needed for stable collagen.
rationales.eli10: Without a helper vitamin, repair ropes are weaker.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A healed scar is paler than surrounding skin. Why?

options.text: Mature scar has fewer blood vessels

rationales.whyCorrect: Vascularity decreases as granulation tissue matures into dense collagen.
rationales.eli10: The temporary supply roads disappear after building ends.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can chronic inflammation cause both tissue destruction and fibrosis?

options.text: Ongoing injury and repair occur together

rationales.whyCorrect: Persistent mediators damage tissue while growth factors stimulate scarring.
rationales.eli10: The area is being damaged and patched at the same time.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What best distinguishes an exudate from a transudate?

options.text: Exudate is protein-rich because permeability increased

rationales.whyCorrect: Inflammatory vessel leak produces protein-rich exudate, unlike pressure-driven transudate.
rationales.eli10: Leaky inflamed vessels let big proteins escape with fluid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A leukocyte adheres firmly after rolling. What interaction is central?

rationales.whyCorrect: Chemokines activate integrins, producing firm endothelial adhesion before transmigration.
rationales.eli10: The rolling cell switches on strong grips to stop.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does scar tissue rarely regain full original strength?

options.text: Collagen is remodeled but original architecture is not perfectly restored

rationales.whyCorrect: Scar organization improves strength but does not recreate intact tissue structure.
rationales.eli10: The patch gets strong, but it is not the original woven fabric.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A mediator causes vasodilation, pain sensitization, and fever. Which class fits?

rationales.whyCorrect: Prostaglandins contribute to vascular, pain, and temperature responses.
rationales.eli10: One alarm chemical family widens roads, hurts, and raises the thermostat.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can diabetes delay wound healing through several pathways?

options.text: Impaired perfusion, immunity, and metabolism hinder repair

rationales.whyCorrect: Vascular disease, altered leukocyte function, and metabolic stress impede coordinated healing.
rationales.eli10: Supply roads, defenders, and builders may all work less effectively.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is edema?

rationales.whyCorrect: Edema is abnormal fluid accumulation outside cells in tissue spaces.
rationales.eli10: Extra water collects between the body's cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is osmosis?

options.text: Water movement across a semipermeable membrane

rationales.whyCorrect: Water moves toward the side with more effective solute concentration.
rationales.eli10: Water crosses a tiny-pore wall toward the saltier side.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which electrolyte is the main extracellular cation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Sodium dominates extracellular fluid and strongly influences its volume and osmolality.
rationales.eli10: Sodium is the main positive particle outside cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Most positive charge inside body cells is carried by which electrolyte?

rationales.whyCorrect: Most body potassium resides inside cells.
rationales.eli10: Potassium is the main positive particle inside cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What pH change defines acidosis?

options.text: A tendency below normal blood pH
A tendency above normal blood pH

rationales.whyCorrect: Acidosis is a process that lowers pH through acid gain or base loss.
rationales.eli10: The blood chemistry is being pushed too sour.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which primary change causes respiratory acidosis?

rationales.whyCorrect: Retained CO2 forms carbonic acid and lowers pH.
rationales.eli10: Trapped carbon dioxide turns into extra acid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which primary change causes metabolic alkalosis?

rationales.whyCorrect: Metabolic alkalosis begins with increased bicarbonate or loss of nonvolatile acid.
rationales.eli10: Losing acid or gaining base makes blood too alkaline.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which ion is essential for muscle and nerve membrane excitability?

rationales.whyCorrect: Potassium gradients strongly influence resting membrane potential.
rationales.eli10: Potassium helps nerves and muscles keep the right electrical charge.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What commonly raises hydrostatic pressure and promotes edema?

rationales.whyCorrect: Elevated venous pressure pushes more fluid out of capillaries.
rationales.eli10: Backed-up pressure squeezes water into nearby tissue.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Profuse diarrhea causes bicarbonate loss. Which disorder may result?

rationales.whyCorrect: Loss of bicarbonate from the intestine lowers blood buffering capacity.
rationales.eli10: Losing base makes the blood more acidic.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Repeated vomiting removes gastric acid. Which disorder may develop?

rationales.whyCorrect: Hydrogen and chloride loss from the stomach raises relative bicarbonate.
rationales.eli10: Throwing away stomach acid leaves the body too basic.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Slow breathing causes carbon dioxide accumulation. Which imbalance follows?

rationales.whyCorrect: Hypoventilation retains CO2, increasing carbonic acid.
rationales.eli10: Breathing too little traps an acid-making gas.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Rapid anxious breathing lowers carbon dioxide. Which imbalance follows?

rationales.whyCorrect: Hyperventilation removes CO2 faster than it is produced, raising pH.
rationales.eli10: Blowing off too much gas removes acid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Low albumin causes edema by changing what force?

rationales.whyCorrect: Albumin normally pulls water into vessels; low levels weaken that inward force.
rationales.eli10: With fewer protein sponges in blood, water leaks into tissue.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Severe hyponatremia can cause brain swelling because what occurs?

rationales.whyCorrect: Low extracellular osmolality drives water intracellularly, including into brain cells.
rationales.eli10: Water moves toward the saltier cell interiors and makes them swell.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Hypernatremia tends to cause which cellular change?

rationales.whyCorrect: High extracellular osmolality draws water out of cells.
rationales.eli10: Salty fluid outside pulls water from cells like a strong sponge.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which concern is most immediate with marked hyperkalemia?

rationales.whyCorrect: Excess potassium alters membrane potentials and can provoke dangerous dysrhythmias.
rationales.eli10: Too much potassium can scramble the heart's electrical timing.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can hypokalemia cause muscle weakness?

options.text: Membranes become abnormally polarized and less excitable

rationales.whyCorrect: Low extracellular potassium makes depolarization more difficult.
rationales.eli10: The muscle's electrical starting point moves too far from its go signal.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A person with dehydration has tachycardia. What is the compensatory purpose?

options.text: Maintain cardiac output despite lower volume

rationales.whyCorrect: A faster heart rate helps preserve flow when stroke volume falls.
rationales.eli10: The heart pumps faster to keep supplies moving with less fluid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Lymphatic obstruction causes limb swelling by what mechanism?

options.text: Impaired return of interstitial fluid and proteins

rationales.whyCorrect: Blocked lymphatics allow protein-rich fluid to remain in tissues.
rationales.eli10: The drainage pipes are blocked, so fluid collects.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In metabolic acidosis, what respiratory compensation is expected?

rationales.whyCorrect: Hyperventilation reduces CO2 and partially raises pH.
rationales.eli10: The lungs blow away acid-making gas.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How do kidneys compensate for chronic respiratory acidosis?

options.text: Retain bicarbonate and excrete more acid

rationales.whyCorrect: Renal hydrogen secretion and bicarbonate retention buffer persistent CO2 elevation.
rationales.eli10: The kidneys save base and send extra acid into urine.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Low calcium increases neuromuscular excitability. Which manifestation fits?

rationales.whyCorrect: Hypocalcemia lowers the threshold for nerve and muscle firing.
rationales.eli10: Nerves become jumpy, making muscles twitch or tingle.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can rapid correction of chronic sodium imbalance be harmful?

options.text: Sodium has no effect on water
Abrupt water shifts can injure adapted brain cells

rationales.whyCorrect: The brain adapts osmotically over time, so rapid reversal can cause damaging shifts.
rationales.eli10: A slowly adjusted brain can be hurt by changing its water balance too fast.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: pH is low, bicarbonate is low, and carbon dioxide is also low. What pattern fits?

rationales.whyCorrect: Low bicarbonate is primary, while low CO2 shows compensatory hyperventilation.
rationales.eli10: Base fell first, and the lungs lowered acid gas to help.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can total-body sodium be high while serum sodium is low in heart failure?

rationales.whyCorrect: Disproportionate water retention dilutes sodium concentration despite expanded volume.
rationales.eli10: There is extra salt, but even more extra water waters it down.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A person has edema, low albumin, and secondary sodium retention. How do these interact?

options.text: Low oncotic pressure promotes leakage while retention expands hydrostatic forces

rationales.whyCorrect: Reduced inward protein force and expanded volume jointly favor tissue fluid accumulation.
rationales.eli10: Weak blood sponges and extra fluid both worsen the puddle.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why may pH be near normal in a mixed acid-base disorder?

options.text: Opposing primary processes can offset pH while both remain abnormal

rationales.whyCorrect: Acidifying and alkalinizing processes may counterbalance the measured pH.
rationales.eli10: Two strong pushes in opposite directions can hide each other.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How can insulin lower serum potassium without removing it from the body?

rationales.whyCorrect: Insulin stimulates cellular potassium uptake through sodium-potassium pumps.
rationales.eli10: Insulin moves potassium from the hallway into cell rooms.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which combination most threatens brain function during acute hyponatremia?

options.text: Rapid water entry and increased intracranial pressure

rationales.whyCorrect: Acute hypotonicity causes cerebral edema within the fixed skull.
rationales.eli10: Swollen brain cells have nowhere to expand inside the hard skull.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which mechanism drives type I hypersensitivity?

rationales.whyCorrect: Type I reactions occur rapidly when allergen cross-links mast-cell-bound IgE.
rationales.eli10: IgE makes alarm cells release chemicals quickly.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What characterizes type II hypersensitivity?

options.text: Antibodies target cell or tissue antigens

rationales.whyCorrect: IgG or IgM binds specific cell-surface or matrix targets and triggers injury or dysfunction.
rationales.eli10: Antibodies mistakenly stick to the body's own structures.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What drives type III hypersensitivity?

rationales.whyCorrect: Antigen-antibody complexes deposit and activate complement and inflammation.
rationales.eli10: Antibody clumps get stuck and start inflammation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A delayed reaction led mainly by sensitized T cells belongs to which hypersensitivity category?

rationales.whyCorrect: Sensitized T cells cause inflammation or cytotoxicity over hours to days.
rationales.eli10: Trained T cells cause a slower reaction.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is autoimmunity?

rationales.whyCorrect: Loss of self-tolerance permits immune injury to the body's own tissues.
rationales.eli10: The defense team mistakes part of the body for an invader.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is immunodeficiency?

rationales.whyCorrect: Defects in immune components increase susceptibility to particular infections.
rationales.eli10: The defense system is missing or weakening some guards.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is sepsis?

options.text: Life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated infection response

rationales.whyCorrect: Sepsis reflects harmful systemic host-response abnormalities causing organ dysfunction.
rationales.eli10: The body's infection alarm becomes so uncontrolled that organs suffer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What defines septic shock conceptually?

options.text: Sepsis with profound circulatory and metabolic abnormalities

rationales.whyCorrect: Septic shock is a severe sepsis subset with persistent perfusion failure and high risk.
rationales.eli10: The infection crisis makes circulation fail dangerously.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is systemic inflammatory response?

rationales.whyCorrect: Systemic mediators alter vessels, metabolism, temperature, and leukocyte activity across the body.
rationales.eli10: The alarm rings throughout the whole building.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Minutes after allergen exposure, wheezing and hives develop. Which reaction fits?

rationales.whyCorrect: Rapid mast-cell mediator release after IgE cross-linking causes these findings.
rationales.eli10: The fast IgE alarm narrows airways and raises itchy bumps.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Antibodies destroy red cells after binding their membranes. Which reaction is this?

rationales.whyCorrect: Antibody-directed injury to cell-surface antigens is type II hypersensitivity.
rationales.eli10: Antibodies put a mistaken target mark on red cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A skin reaction peaks two days after antigen contact. Which type fits?

rationales.whyCorrect: Delayed T-cell recruitment commonly produces type IV reactions after 48 to 72 hours.
rationales.eli10: T cells need time to gather, so the rash appears later.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can immune complexes injure kidneys?

options.text: They deposit in glomeruli and activate inflammation

rationales.whyCorrect: Filtered vascular beds trap complexes, provoking complement and leukocyte damage.
rationales.eli10: Tiny antibody clumps lodge in kidney filters and summon an attack.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Loss of helper T cells increases opportunistic infections because what fails?

options.text: Coordination of cellular and antibody responses

rationales.whyCorrect: Helper T cells activate multiple adaptive immune partners.
rationales.eli10: Without the coach, several defense teams work poorly.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A localized infection progresses to confusion and reduced urine output. What is concerning?

rationales.whyCorrect: Altered mentation and kidney dysfunction indicate systemic harm during infection.
rationales.eli10: The alarm is now affecting the brain and kidneys.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can sepsis cause hypotension?

options.text: Vasodilation and capillary leakage reduce effective circulation

rationales.whyCorrect: Inflammatory mediators widen vessels and shift fluid out of the bloodstream.
rationales.eli10: Wide leaky pipes leave too little pressure to deliver blood.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A genetic complement defect causes recurrent bacterial infections. Why?

options.text: Opsonization and microbial lysis are impaired

rationales.whyCorrect: Complement helps label and directly damage susceptible bacteria.
rationales.eli10: One tagging and punching system is missing.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can autoimmune disease alternate between flares and remission?

options.text: Triggers and regulatory balance vary over time

rationales.whyCorrect: Infections, hormones, therapy, and immune regulation can shift disease activity.
rationales.eli10: The mistaken alarm can grow louder or quieter over time.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An inherited B-cell defect most directly reduces what?

rationales.whyCorrect: B cells differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells.
rationales.eli10: Without B cells, the body makes fewer matching shields.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Persistent hypotension reduces organ oxygen delivery in septic shock. What may rise?

rationales.whyCorrect: Poor perfusion encourages anaerobic metabolism and lactate accumulation.
rationales.eli10: Starved cells use a backup pathway that leaves lactate.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can fever help host defense within limits?

options.text: It can inhibit some microbes and enhance immune reactions

rationales.whyCorrect: Moderate temperature elevation can make conditions less favorable for pathogens and support immunity.
rationales.eli10: Turning up the heat can slow some germs and energize defenders.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An immunosuppressive drug increases infection risk. What tradeoff is involved?

options.text: Reduced harmful immunity also weakens protection

rationales.whyCorrect: Suppressing excessive or transplanted-tissue responses can impair antimicrobial defenses.
rationales.eli10: Quieting an overactive guard can make intruders easier to miss.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why may severe infection trigger abnormal clotting throughout small vessels?

options.text: Inflammation activates coagulation and injures endothelium

rationales.whyCorrect: Inflammation and tissue-factor pathways can produce microthrombi and consume clotting components.
rationales.eli10: The alarm makes tiny clots everywhere and uses up repair supplies.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which finding best suggests distributive rather than hypovolemic shock early in sepsis?

rationales.whyCorrect: Early septic vasodilation can produce warm extremities despite poor effective perfusion.
rationales.eli10: Pipes open wide, so skin feels warm while pressure falls.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How can molecular mimicry promote autoimmunity?

options.text: Microbial antigens resemble self and activate cross-reactive lymphocytes

rationales.whyCorrect: A response against a pathogen may recognize similar host epitopes.
rationales.eli10: A germ's disguise resembles the body, so defenders hit both.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why may septic organs fail despite adequate blood oxygen content?

options.text: Microcirculatory and cellular oxygen use are disrupted

rationales.whyCorrect: Shunting, endothelial injury, edema, and mitochondrial dysfunction impair delivery and use.
rationales.eli10: Supply trucks carry oxygen, but damaged side roads and factories cannot use it.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A reaction contains antibody, complement, and neutrophils around deposited complexes. Which type is integrated here?

rationales.whyCorrect: Type III injury follows immune-complex deposition and complement-driven inflammation.
rationales.eli10: Stuck antibody bundles call complement and cleanup cells that damage tissue.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can late sepsis include immune suppression as well as inflammation?

options.text: Cell exhaustion and anti-inflammatory pathways reduce defense

rationales.whyCorrect: Dysregulation can shift toward lymphocyte loss and impaired pathogen clearance.
rationales.eli10: After an enormous alarm, the defense team may become exhausted.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which observation best distinguishes colonization from infection?

options.text: Tissue invasion or host damage accompanies microbial presence

rationales.whyCorrect: Infection implies invasion and host response or injury, not mere occupancy.
rationales.eli10: A neighbor becomes an invader when it damages the home.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How can a primary immunodeficiency produce a recognizable infection pattern?

options.text: The missing immune component leaves vulnerability to particular pathogen types

rationales.whyCorrect: Different arms control different microbes, so the defect shapes susceptibility.
rationales.eli10: Missing a certain guard leaves the gate it watched especially open.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which feature is typical of a benign tumor?

rationales.whyCorrect: Benign neoplasms usually remain localized and do not metastasize.
rationales.eli10: The lump grows in its neighborhood instead of traveling.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What defines a malignant tumor?

rationales.whyCorrect: Malignant cells infiltrate tissue and may establish distant tumors.
rationales.eli10: These cells can break boundaries and start colonies elsewhere.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is metastasis?

options.text: Spread of cancer to a discontinuous site

rationales.whyCorrect: Metastasis forms secondary tumors separate from the primary mass.
rationales.eli10: Cancer cells travel and build a new harmful home.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What does tumor grade primarily describe?

rationales.whyCorrect: Grade assesses how abnormal and proliferative tumor cells appear.
rationales.eli10: It measures how wild the cells look under a microscope.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which tumor measure maps the anatomic extent of disease?

rationales.whyCorrect: Stage summarizes primary size, nodal involvement, and distant spread.
rationales.eli10: It maps how far the cancer has traveled.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is an oncogene?

rationales.whyCorrect: Oncogenes arise when proto-oncogenes become overactive or altered.
rationales.eli10: A stuck gas pedal tells cells to keep growing.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What does a tumor suppressor gene normally do?

options.text: Restrain growth or protect genome integrity

rationales.whyCorrect: Tumor suppressors regulate checkpoints, repair damage, or trigger apoptosis.
rationales.eli10: It is a brake and safety inspector for cell growth.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is carcinogenesis?

rationales.whyCorrect: Carcinogenesis accumulates genetic and epigenetic changes that enable malignant behavior.
rationales.eli10: Several broken rules slowly turn a normal cell into cancer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is a tumor marker?

options.text: A measurable substance associated with some tumors

rationales.whyCorrect: Markers may aid monitoring or evaluation but often lack perfect specificity.
rationales.eli10: It is a clue in blood or tissue, not a final answer alone.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A mass expands but has a smooth capsule and no invasion. Which behavior is suggested?

rationales.whyCorrect: Well-circumscribed noninvasive growth favors a benign neoplasm.
rationales.eli10: The growth stays behind a clear fence.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Tumor cells enter lymphatic vessels. What capability does this demonstrate?

rationales.whyCorrect: Penetrating vessels is a necessary step toward distant dissemination.
rationales.eli10: The cells broke into a travel route.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A biopsy shows highly abnormal cells unlike their tissue of origin. How is this described?

rationales.whyCorrect: Loss of specialized morphology indicates poor differentiation and often higher grade.
rationales.eli10: The cells have forgotten what normal job and shape they should have.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can loss of p53 promote cancer?

options.text: Damaged cells continue cycling instead of repairing or dying

rationales.whyCorrect: p53 normally pauses damaged cells or initiates apoptosis.
rationales.eli10: The safety inspector is gone, so damaged cells keep copying.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A growth-factor receptor signals without ligand. What kind of alteration is this?

rationales.whyCorrect: Constitutive signaling drives proliferation without normal external control.
rationales.eli10: The growth switch is jammed on without anyone pressing it.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why must a growing tumor stimulate angiogenesis?

rationales.whyCorrect: Diffusion alone cannot supply an enlarging tumor, so new vessels support it.
rationales.eli10: A growing city needs new supply roads.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Cancer is found in a distant organ but resembles the primary tumor. What is it?

rationales.whyCorrect: Distant cells retain features of their tissue of origin.
rationales.eli10: Traveling cancer cells built another colony.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why may a tumor marker fall after effective therapy?

rationales.whyCorrect: For a marker produced by that tumor, serial decline can reflect fewer tumor cells.
rationales.eli10: Fewer cancer factories release less of the clue.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is one elevated tumor marker not diagnostic by itself?

options.text: Benign conditions may also raise it

rationales.whyCorrect: Limited specificity means results require clinical, imaging, and tissue context.
rationales.eli10: A clue can have more than one explanation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A tumor compresses nearby tissue but does not penetrate it. Which property is absent?

rationales.whyCorrect: Invasion requires infiltration across normal tissue boundaries.
rationales.eli10: The mass pushes the fence but does not cross it.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can inherited DNA-repair defects raise cancer risk?

rationales.whyCorrect: Impaired repair creates genomic instability across many cell generations.
rationales.eli10: Spelling mistakes pile up when the proofreader is missing.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Chronic tissue inflammation promotes carcinogenesis partly through what?

options.text: Repeated injury, cell turnover, and reactive molecules

rationales.whyCorrect: Ongoing damage and proliferation increase opportunities for transforming changes.
rationales.eli10: Constant damage and rebuilding create more chances for bad instructions.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A tumor has small size but distant metastases. Which measure captures this seriousness?

rationales.whyCorrect: Distant spread produces an advanced stage even when the primary is small.
rationales.eli10: A small starting fire is serious if sparks started fires far away.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which change helps cancer cells avoid apoptosis?

rationales.whyCorrect: Blocking programmed death allows abnormal cells to survive stress and therapy.
rationales.eli10: The faulty cell disables its self-destruct button.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can cancer cause weight and muscle loss even with adequate intake?

options.text: Inflammatory and metabolic signals drive catabolism

rationales.whyCorrect: Cancer-associated mediators can alter appetite and accelerate tissue breakdown.
rationales.eli10: The illness changes body signals so stores are burned too quickly.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does malignancy usually require multiple genetic changes?

options.text: Cells need several growth, survival, and invasion controls disrupted
One mutation always supplies every capability

rationales.whyCorrect: Cancer evolves as alterations jointly enable hallmark behaviors.
rationales.eli10: Several safety systems must fail before the cell becomes a dangerous traveler.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A high-grade tumor remains localized. How should grade and stage be interpreted?

options.text: Cells look aggressive, but anatomic spread is limited

rationales.whyCorrect: Grade and stage measure different dimensions and need not match.
rationales.eli10: The cells look wild, yet the map shows they have not traveled.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How does epithelial-mesenchymal transition support metastasis?

options.text: It increases motility and reduces cell-cell attachment

rationales.whyCorrect: This program enables epithelial tumor cells to detach and invade.
rationales.eli10: Stationary brick-like cells become more like moving explorers.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can tumor heterogeneity cause therapy resistance?

options.text: Preexisting resistant subclones may survive and expand

rationales.whyCorrect: Genetically diverse cells respond differently, allowing selection of resistant populations.
rationales.eli10: Medicine removes weak weeds while tougher ones remain and spread.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which evidence most directly distinguishes recurrence from a new primary tumor?

options.text: Molecular features match the earlier tumor
Both occur in the same person

rationales.whyCorrect: Shared distinctive mutations support descent from the original cancer.
rationales.eli10: Matching rare spelling errors show the tumors share an ancestor.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can blocking one growth pathway have only temporary effect?

options.text: Alternate pathways or resistant clones can bypass the block

rationales.whyCorrect: Adaptive signaling and clonal selection can restore proliferation.
rationales.eli10: Cancer may take a detour around one closed road.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is hypertension?

rationales.whyCorrect: Hypertension chronically increases force against arterial walls.
rationales.eli10: Blood pushes through the pipes with too much pressure.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What begins atherosclerotic plaque development?

rationales.whyCorrect: Endothelial dysfunction permits lipid accumulation and inflammatory recruitment.
rationales.eli10: Damage to the pipe lining lets fat and defenders gather.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is angina?

options.text: Chest discomfort from transient myocardial ischemia

rationales.whyCorrect: Angina reflects temporary mismatch between cardiac oxygen supply and demand without necrosis.
rationales.eli10: The heart hurts when it briefly needs more oxygen than it gets.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What distinguishes myocardial infarction from stable angina?

rationales.whyCorrect: Infarction kills heart muscle, whereas stable angina is reversible ischemia.
rationales.eli10: A long supply cutoff kills cells instead of only making them struggle.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is cardiac output?

options.text: Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume

rationales.whyCorrect: Cardiac output is the volume pumped per minute: HR × SV.
rationales.eli10: Beats per minute times blood per beat equals flow per minute.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What does perfusion mean?

rationales.whyCorrect: Perfusion supplies cells with oxygen and nutrients through blood flow.
rationales.eli10: It is the delivery of fresh blood to working cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which side of heart failure commonly causes pulmonary congestion?

rationales.whyCorrect: Left ventricular failure raises pressure backward into pulmonary vessels.
rationales.eli10: A weak left pump backs fluid toward the lungs.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is a dysrhythmia?

rationales.whyCorrect: Dysrhythmias arise from abnormal impulse formation or conduction.
rationales.eli10: The heart's electrical beat pattern is off.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What defines shock?

options.text: Only low blood pressure without effects

rationales.whyCorrect: Shock is circulatory failure that cannot meet cellular metabolic needs.
rationales.eli10: Not enough blood reaches cells with supplies.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An artery narrows from plaque. Why may exertion cause chest discomfort?

options.text: Heart oxygen demand exceeds limited supply

rationales.whyCorrect: Fixed narrowing may supply rest needs but not increased exercise demand.
rationales.eli10: A narrow road works at quiet times but jams during rush hour.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A coronary plaque ruptures. What event most directly causes acute infarction?

rationales.whyCorrect: Rupture exposes thrombogenic material, producing an occluding clot.
rationales.eli10: A cracked plaque triggers a blood plug that blocks the artery.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The left ventricle cannot empty effectively. What changes?

rationales.whyCorrect: Poor systolic contraction leaves more blood in the ventricle after ejection.
rationales.eli10: The weak pump leaves extra blood behind each beat.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does chronic hypertension promote ventricular hypertrophy?

options.text: The ventricle pumps against greater afterload

rationales.whyCorrect: Pressure overload increases wall stress and drives myocyte enlargement.
rationales.eli10: Heart cells bulk up to push against a heavier door.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Right-sided heart failure commonly produces which finding?

rationales.whyCorrect: Systemic venous pressure rises and pushes fluid into dependent tissues.
rationales.eli10: Blood backs up in body veins, so ankles may swell.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A very fast dysrhythmia lowers cardiac output. Why?

rationales.whyCorrect: Short diastole reduces preload and stroke volume.
rationales.eli10: The chambers do not get enough refill time between fast beats.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Severe blood loss causes which type of shock?

rationales.whyCorrect: Loss of circulating volume reduces venous return and output.
rationales.eli10: There is not enough fluid left in the circulation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A large myocardial infarction causes pump failure and hypotension. Which shock fits?

rationales.whyCorrect: Cardiogenic shock results from inadequate cardiac pumping despite circulating volume.
rationales.eli10: The tank has blood, but the pump is too damaged.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Widespread vasodilation in sepsis produces which shock category?

rationales.whyCorrect: Distributive shock features loss of vascular tone and maldistributed flow.
rationales.eli10: The pipes open too wide, so pressure and delivery fail.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A massive pulmonary embolus blocks right-heart outflow. Which shock fits?

rationales.whyCorrect: Mechanical blockage of circulation causes obstructive shock.
rationales.eli10: A clot blocks the route even though the pump and fluid are present.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does heart failure activate sodium retention?

options.text: Blood volume is always excessive at kidneys

rationales.whyCorrect: Neurohormonal systems interpret renal hypoperfusion as low volume and retain sodium and water.
rationales.eli10: The kidneys mistake weak delivery for an empty tank and save fluid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can atherosclerosis cause symptoms in many organs?

options.text: It occurs only in the heart

rationales.whyCorrect: Plaques can narrow vessels supplying heart, brain, limbs, kidneys, and other tissues.
rationales.eli10: The same pipe disease can block roads in many neighborhoods.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A person has cool skin during hypovolemic shock. What explains it?

rationales.whyCorrect: Sympathetic constriction redirects limited flow toward vital organs.
rationales.eli10: The body closes skin roads to save blood for the brain and heart.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does pulmonary edema impair oxygenation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Fluid between alveolar gas and capillary blood slows oxygen transfer.
rationales.eli10: Oxygen must cross a waterlogged wall.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Long-standing low perfusion raises lactate. What process produces it?

rationales.whyCorrect: Oxygen-starved cells convert pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+.
rationales.eli10: Cells use a backup sugar path and leave lactate behind.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can systolic pressure be maintained early in shock despite falling volume?

rationales.whyCorrect: Neural and hormonal responses temporarily preserve pressure and output.
rationales.eli10: The heart speeds up and pipes tighten to hide the falling supply.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A normal ejection fraction coexists with heart-failure symptoms. What can explain this?

options.text: A stiff ventricle fills poorly despite preserved fractional ejection

rationales.whyCorrect: Diastolic dysfunction can raise filling pressures and limit output while EF remains preserved.
rationales.eli10: The pump squeezes well but its stiff chamber will not fill easily.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How does plaque rupture differ from gradual stenosis clinically?

options.text: Rupture can trigger sudden thrombosis on a previously moderate lesion

rationales.whyCorrect: Acute clot formation can abruptly occlude a plaque that was not severely obstructive.
rationales.eli10: A modest bump can suddenly become a roadblock when a clot forms.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why may vasopressors improve pressure but not fully restore tissue perfusion?

options.text: Pressure and microcirculatory flow are identical
Constricted or damaged microvessels may still distribute flow poorly

rationales.whyCorrect: Macroscopic pressure does not guarantee effective capillary oxygen delivery.
rationales.eli10: Raising main-pipe pressure does not fix every damaged side street.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A failing heart remodels and dilates. Why can compensation become harmful?

options.text: Wall stress and oxygen demand rise, worsening function

rationales.whyCorrect: Chronic remodeling initially preserves output but eventually increases mechanical burden.
rationales.eli10: Stretching the pump helps briefly, then makes its job harder.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which relationship explains why bradycardia can lower output despite normal stroke volume?

options.text: Output equals heart rate times stroke volume
Output equals oxygen divided by sodium

rationales.whyCorrect: Too few beats per minute reduce total flow even if each beat is normal.
rationales.eli10: Good-sized scoops still move little water if scooping is too slow.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the primary reversible airflow problem in asthma?

rationales.whyCorrect: Asthma narrows hyperresponsive airways through smooth-muscle contraction, edema, and mucus.
rationales.eli10: The breathing tubes tighten and swell but can reopen.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What structural change defines emphysema?

rationales.whyCorrect: Emphysema enlarges airspaces and reduces elastic and gas-exchange surface.
rationales.eli10: Tiny air balloons merge into bigger, floppier ones.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What characterizes chronic bronchitis clinically?

rationales.whyCorrect: Mucus hypersecretion and bronchial inflammation cause persistent productive cough.
rationales.eli10: Irritated tubes keep making mucus that must be coughed up.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is pneumonia?

options.text: Infection and inflammation of lung tissue

rationales.whyCorrect: Pneumonia fills affected alveoli with inflammatory material.
rationales.eli10: Germs and defenders fill air sacs that should hold air.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is a pulmonary embolism?

rationales.whyCorrect: Most pulmonary emboli are clots that travel to pulmonary circulation.
rationales.eli10: A traveling clot plugs a blood road in the lungs.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What does hypoxemia mean?

rationales.whyCorrect: Hypoxemia is reduced oxygen in arterial blood.
rationales.eli10: The blood leaving the lungs carries too little oxygen.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is ventilation?

options.text: Movement of air into and out of alveoli

rationales.whyCorrect: Ventilation refreshes alveolar gas through breathing.
rationales.eli10: It is moving fresh air in and used air out.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is perfusion in the lung?

rationales.whyCorrect: Pulmonary perfusion brings blood beside ventilated alveoli for gas exchange.
rationales.eli10: Blood travels past air sacs to pick up oxygen.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is ARDS?

options.text: Diffuse inflammatory lung injury with noncardiogenic edema

rationales.whyCorrect: ARDS increases alveolar-capillary permeability and causes severe oxygenation failure.
rationales.eli10: Leaky inflamed lungs become wet and hard to oxygenate.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Wheezing improves after a bronchodilator. Which mechanism was reversed?

rationales.whyCorrect: Relaxing bronchial smooth muscle widens airflow pathways in asthma.
rationales.eli10: The medicine loosens the squeezed breathing tubes.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is exhalation difficult in emphysema?

options.text: Loss of elastic recoil promotes airway collapse

rationales.whyCorrect: Reduced recoil and radial support trap air during expiration.
rationales.eli10: Floppy tubes close before stale air gets out.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Consolidated alveoli are perfused but poorly ventilated. What occurs?

rationales.whyCorrect: Blood passes airspaces containing fluid rather than fresh gas.
rationales.eli10: Blood visits a wet air sac that cannot give it enough oxygen.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A pulmonary embolus blocks flow to ventilated alveoli. What results?

rationales.whyCorrect: Air reaches alveoli that lack corresponding blood flow.
rationales.eli10: Fresh air arrives, but no blood truck comes to collect oxygen.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can pneumonia cause crackles?

options.text: Air moves through fluid-containing small airways and alveoli

rationales.whyCorrect: Opening fluid-lined airspaces produces discontinuous crackling sounds.
rationales.eli10: Air bubbles through wet tiny spaces like fizzing wrap.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which early change in ARDS drives refractory hypoxemia?

rationales.whyCorrect: Shunt-like perfusion of nonventilated units responds incompletely to added oxygen.
rationales.eli10: Blood passes many collapsed wet air sacs.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can chronic bronchitis cause hypoxemia?

options.text: Obstructed inflamed airways create V-Q mismatch

rationales.whyCorrect: Poor ventilation of still-perfused lung regions lowers oxygenation.
rationales.eli10: Mucus blocks air roads while blood keeps passing nearby.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A person suddenly develops dyspnea after a leg clot. What mechanism is likely?

rationales.whyCorrect: A venous thrombus can travel through the right heart into pulmonary arteries.
rationales.eli10: A clot breaks loose and rides to the lung vessels.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does severe asthma increase work of breathing?

rationales.whyCorrect: Small decreases in airway radius greatly increase resistance to airflow.
rationales.eli10: Pushing air through a skinny straw takes more effort.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A low diffusion capacity in emphysema reflects what loss?

rationales.whyCorrect: Destroyed septa reduce area available for gas transfer.
rationales.eli10: Fewer tiny air-sac walls mean less room for oxygen to cross.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why may a severe pneumonia increase respiratory rate?

options.text: Compensation attempts to improve gas exchange

rationales.whyCorrect: Hypoxemia and increased work stimulate faster breathing.
rationales.eli10: The body speeds the bellows to bring in more oxygen.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which pattern suggests airway obstruction?

rationales.whyCorrect: Obstructive disorders disproportionately limit rapid exhalation.
rationales.eli10: The narrowed exit slows air leaving the lungs.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How does surfactant loss worsen ARDS?

options.text: It raises surface tension and promotes collapse

rationales.whyCorrect: Surfactant normally lowers surface tension and stabilizes alveoli.
rationales.eli10: Without the slippery coating, tiny air sacs stick shut.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can supplemental oxygen help V-Q mismatch more than a complete shunt?

options.text: Some air still reaches low-ventilation units

rationales.whyCorrect: Raising inspired oxygen can improve partially ventilated regions but not blood bypassing air entirely.
rationales.eli10: Extra oxygen helps a weakly open room, not a room with no doorway.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A person retains CO2 during advanced COPD. What failed?

rationales.whyCorrect: Insufficient effective ventilation prevents removal of produced carbon dioxide.
rationales.eli10: The lungs cannot blow out the used gas fast enough.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can oxygenation remain poor in ARDS despite high inspired oxygen?

options.text: Perfusion continues through nonventilated collapsed units

rationales.whyCorrect: Intrapulmonary shunting bypasses functioning gas-exchange surfaces.
rationales.eli10: Some blood takes a route past closed air sacs.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How can pulmonary embolism strain the right ventricle?

options.text: It abruptly raises pulmonary vascular resistance

rationales.whyCorrect: The right ventricle must pump against an acutely obstructed pulmonary circuit.
rationales.eli10: The right pump suddenly faces a blocked, high-pressure road.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A person with emphysema and pneumonia develops worse hypoxemia. Why?

options.text: Surface loss and low-V-Q units compound gas-exchange failure

rationales.whyCorrect: Emphysematous destruction plus fluid-filled units jointly reduce effective exchange.
rationales.eli10: Fewer working walls and newly flooded sacs leave even less oxygen space.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can dynamic hyperinflation occur during rapid breathing in obstruction?

options.text: The next breath begins before full exhalation

rationales.whyCorrect: Short expiratory time traps progressively more gas.
rationales.eli10: New air arrives before the old air has finished leaving.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which change makes alveolar oxygen transfer slower even with ventilation present?

rationales.whyCorrect: A thicker diffusion path reduces gas-transfer rate.
rationales.eli10: Oxygen crosses a thick wall more slowly than a thin one.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why may severe asthma become life-threatening when wheezing grows quiet?

options.text: Minimal airflow may be producing little sound

rationales.whyCorrect: A nearly closed airway moves too little air to generate wheezing.
rationales.eli10: A very blocked straw may become silent because almost no air moves.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is glomerular filtration?

options.text: Movement of plasma water and small solutes into Bowman's space

rationales.whyCorrect: Pressure filters small components across the glomerular barrier into the nephron.
rationales.eli10: The kidney sieve lets water and tiny particles enter a tube.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What defines acute kidney injury?

rationales.whyCorrect: AKI develops over hours to days with reduced filtration and waste handling.
rationales.eli10: The kidney filters suddenly slow down.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What defines chronic kidney disease?

options.text: Persistent kidney damage or low function

rationales.whyCorrect: CKD persists for months and often progresses with nephron loss.
rationales.eli10: Kidney damage lasts a long time instead of passing quickly.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is proteinuria?

rationales.whyCorrect: Proteinuria reflects abnormal filtration barrier leakage or impaired reabsorption.
rationales.eli10: Protein slips through a filter that should keep it in blood.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is hematuria?

rationales.whyCorrect: Hematuria indicates bleeding somewhere along the urinary tract.
rationales.eli10: Red blood cells have entered the urine pathway.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is a urinary tract infection?

rationales.whyCorrect: UTIs involve microbial growth in urethra, bladder, ureters, or kidneys.
rationales.eli10: Germs are growing somewhere along the urine plumbing.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which finding is central to nephrotic syndrome?

rationales.whyCorrect: Major glomerular protein loss drives hypoalbuminemia, edema, and lipid changes.
rationales.eli10: A very leaky filter loses lots of protein.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which process is typical of glomerulonephritis?

rationales.whyCorrect: Immune or inflammatory damage reduces filtration and permits blood and protein leakage.
rationales.eli10: The kidney's tiny filters become inflamed.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which hormone made by kidneys supports red-cell production?

rationales.whyCorrect: Renal erythropoietin stimulates bone marrow erythrocyte production.
rationales.eli10: Kidneys send a message telling marrow to make red cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Severe dehydration reduces renal blood flow. Which AKI type fits?

rationales.whyCorrect: Prerenal AKI begins with inadequate perfusion before structural kidney damage.
rationales.eli10: The filter lacks incoming water pressure.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A toxin directly damages renal tubules. Which AKI category fits?

rationales.whyCorrect: Injury within renal tissue is intrinsic AKI.
rationales.eli10: The kidney's own tubes are damaged.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Bilateral urinary obstruction causes which AKI type?

rationales.whyCorrect: Blocked outflow raises pressure backward and reduces net filtration.
rationales.eli10: A clogged exit backs pressure up to the filters.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does nephrotic syndrome cause edema?

options.text: Urinary albumin loss lowers plasma oncotic pressure

rationales.whyCorrect: Low plasma albumin weakens the force retaining water in vessels.
rationales.eli10: Lost blood protein means fewer sponges holding water inside vessels.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A lower UTI causes urinary frequency and burning. Which site is commonly involved?

rationales.whyCorrect: Cystitis irritates bladder mucosa, producing urgency, frequency, and dysuria.
rationales.eli10: An inflamed urine-storage bag feels urgent and sore.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why may kidney infection cause flank pain and fever?

rationales.whyCorrect: Pyelonephritis involves the renal pelvis and parenchyma, provoking systemic response.
rationales.eli10: The infection has climbed into the kidney itself.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: As GFR falls, which waste commonly accumulates?

rationales.whyCorrect: Reduced filtration decreases creatinine clearance, raising its blood concentration.
rationales.eli10: A slower sieve leaves more waste in the bloodstream.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can CKD cause anemia?

rationales.whyCorrect: Damaged kidneys provide less marrow-stimulating hormone.
rationales.eli10: The marrow receives fewer make-red-cells messages.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can renal failure produce hyperkalemia?

rationales.whyCorrect: Low filtration and secretion reduce urinary potassium removal.
rationales.eli10: The kidneys cannot send enough potassium out in urine.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Glomerular inflammation permits red cells to enter urine. What finding may appear?

rationales.whyCorrect: Red cells molded within renal tubules form casts, pointing to glomerular bleeding.
rationales.eli10: Red cells clump into tube-shaped clues inside kidney channels.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does sodium retention worsen kidney-related edema?

rationales.whyCorrect: Sodium expands extracellular volume because water accompanies it.
rationales.eli10: Saved salt pulls saved water along.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A person with AKI has low urine output. What imbalance needs close monitoring?

rationales.whyCorrect: Limited urine excretion allows water, potassium, and acids to accumulate.
rationales.eli10: A blocked drain lets fluid and wastes pile up.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can CKD produce metabolic acidosis?

options.text: Kidneys excrete less acid and regenerate less bicarbonate

rationales.whyCorrect: Declining nephrons cannot maintain normal acid-base balance.
rationales.eli10: Weak filters cannot throw away enough acid or refill base.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which change follows reduced activation of vitamin D in CKD?

rationales.whyCorrect: Diseased kidneys make less calcitriol, disrupting calcium and bone regulation.
rationales.eli10: Without activated vitamin D, the gut opens fewer calcium doors.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An obstruction is relieved early. Why may kidney function recover?

options.text: Structural damage may not yet be irreversible

rationales.whyCorrect: Prompt restoration of outflow can normalize filtration before sustained pressure causes loss.
rationales.eli10: Opening the clog early lets the filters restart.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can prerenal AKI become intrinsic AKI if prolonged?

rationales.whyCorrect: Sustained hypoperfusion causes ischemic acute tubular injury.
rationales.eli10: A long supply shortage eventually damages the filter machinery.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How can severe proteinuria increase thrombosis risk?

options.text: Urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins shifts balance toward clotting

rationales.whyCorrect: Loss of antithrombin and other regulators contributes to hypercoagulability.
rationales.eli10: Important anti-clot guards leak out with the protein.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A person with CKD has high phosphate and low calcium. What response follows?

rationales.whyCorrect: Mineral imbalance stimulates PTH, which increases bone turnover.
rationales.eli10: The body pulls calcium from bone when blood levels stay low.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can serum creatinine lag behind an abrupt fall in GFR?

options.text: Blood accumulation takes time to reach a new steady level

rationales.whyCorrect: Creatinine concentration changes over time after filtration suddenly declines.
rationales.eli10: The waste pile needs time to become visibly larger.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which combination best differentiates nephritic from nephrotic patterns?

options.text: Prominent hematuria and inflammation rather than massive protein loss

rationales.whyCorrect: Nephritic injury emphasizes inflammatory bleeding and reduced filtration.
rationales.eli10: An inflamed filter leaks blood; a very porous filter leaks lots of protein.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does progressive CKD continue after the original injury resolves?

options.text: Hyperfiltration stresses surviving nephrons and promotes scarring

rationales.whyCorrect: Compensatory workload within remaining nephrons can accelerate further damage.
rationales.eli10: Fewer filters work overtime until the extra strain harms them too.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What causes an ischemic stroke?

rationales.whyCorrect: A thrombus or embolus deprives brain tissue of oxygen and glucose.
rationales.eli10: A plug blocks a supply road to part of the brain.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What causes a hemorrhagic stroke?

options.text: Bleeding into or around the brain

rationales.whyCorrect: A ruptured vessel releases blood that damages and compresses brain tissue.
rationales.eli10: A brain blood pipe breaks and leaks.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is a transient ischemic attack?

options.text: Temporary focal dysfunction without acute infarction

rationales.whyCorrect: A TIA resolves because blood-flow interruption does not produce detectable infarction.
rationales.eli10: The brain's supply flickers off briefly without leaving dead tissue.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is a seizure?

options.text: Abnormal excessive synchronized brain electrical activity

rationales.whyCorrect: Seizures result from transient pathologic neuronal firing.
rationales.eli10: Many brain cells fire together at the wrong time.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is intracranial pressure?

rationales.whyCorrect: Brain tissue, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid share the rigid cranial space.
rationales.eli10: It is the squeeze inside the hard skull box.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which disease features progressive memory and cognitive decline with amyloid and tau pathology?

rationales.whyCorrect: Alzheimer's disease is a neurodegenerative dementia linked to amyloid plaques and tau tangles.
rationales.eli10: Brain networks slowly lose connections used for memory and thinking.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Loss of dopamine neurons is central to which disorder?

rationales.whyCorrect: Degeneration of substantia nigra dopamine neurons disrupts basal-ganglia movement circuits.
rationales.eli10: Loss of a movement messenger makes starting and controlling motion harder.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which deficit is aphasia?

rationales.whyCorrect: Aphasia affects production or comprehension of language after dominant-hemisphere injury.
rationales.eli10: The brain has trouble using or understanding words.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is traumatic brain injury?

options.text: Brain dysfunction caused by external force

rationales.whyCorrect: Impact, acceleration, penetration, or blast forces can disrupt brain function.
rationales.eli10: An outside force shakes, strikes, or injures the brain.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Sudden right-arm weakness and aphasia suggest injury to which side?

rationales.whyCorrect: Motor pathways cross, and language is commonly left-lateralized.
rationales.eli10: The left brain often handles words and controls the right side.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can a brain hemorrhage rapidly worsen neurological function?

options.text: Blood adds mass and raises pressure

rationales.whyCorrect: Bleeding compresses tissue within a fixed space and reduces perfusion.
rationales.eli10: Leaking blood takes up room in a box that cannot stretch.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A seizure affects one hand while awareness remains intact. What type is suggested?

rationales.whyCorrect: Localized cortical firing can cause focal motor signs without loss of awareness.
rationales.eli10: One small brain area misfires, so one body part moves.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does cerebral edema raise intracranial pressure?

options.text: The skull cannot expand to hold extra volume

rationales.whyCorrect: Added tissue water increases total volume within the rigid cranium.
rationales.eli10: Extra swelling has nowhere to go inside the hard shell.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A head injury is followed by a lucid interval and rapid decline. What concern is classic?

rationales.whyCorrect: Arterial bleeding can enlarge after a temporary symptom-free period.
rationales.eli10: A hidden blood pocket grows after the person briefly seems well.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why may stroke deficits appear on the side opposite the lesion?

options.text: Major motor pathways cross in the brainstem

rationales.whyCorrect: Corticospinal fibers decussate, so one hemisphere controls the opposite side.
rationales.eli10: Movement wires cross, like cords switching sides.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A TIA resolves. Why is it still important?

options.text: It can warn of future ischemic stroke

rationales.whyCorrect: Transient symptoms may reveal unstable vascular disease with elevated later risk.
rationales.eli10: A brief road blockage warns that a lasting one may come.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which change produces Parkinsonian bradykinesia?

rationales.whyCorrect: Basal-ganglia imbalance makes initiating and scaling movement difficult.
rationales.eli10: The brain's movement-starting signal becomes too weak.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does Alzheimer's disease eventually impair daily tasks?

rationales.whyCorrect: Neuronal and synaptic loss spreads through networks for memory, reasoning, and function.
rationales.eli10: More thinking pathways disconnect, making familiar jobs difficult.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A person ignores the left side after right parietal stroke. What deficit is this?

rationales.whyCorrect: Right parietal attention-network injury can impair awareness of left space.
rationales.eli10: The brain's map stops noticing one side of the world.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can prolonged seizures cause neuronal injury?

options.text: Sustained firing raises energy demand and excitotoxic stress

rationales.whyCorrect: Continuous activity can outstrip supply and cause calcium-mediated damage.
rationales.eli10: Brain cells race without rest until fuel and control fail.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which change may indicate rising intracranial pressure?

rationales.whyCorrect: Compression and reduced cerebral perfusion often impair consciousness.
rationales.eli10: A squeezed brain becomes less able to stay awake.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A cerebellar lesion most likely causes what?

rationales.whyCorrect: The cerebellum calibrates movement timing, accuracy, and posture.
rationales.eli10: The movement coach can no longer smooth and balance actions.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can ischemic tissue surrounding an infarct sometimes be saved?

options.text: It receives no blood at all
The penumbra is impaired but not irreversibly injured

rationales.whyCorrect: Collateral flow may sustain penumbral cells temporarily, making rapid reperfusion valuable.
rationales.eli10: Nearby cells are struggling but not dead yet.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: After head trauma, a person cannot form new memories. Which region may be affected?

rationales.whyCorrect: The hippocampus is central to consolidating new declarative memories.
rationales.eli10: The brain's save button for new memories is damaged.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can lowering systemic blood pressure too far worsen elevated-ICP injury?

rationales.whyCorrect: Cerebral perfusion depends on mean arterial pressure relative to intracranial pressure.
rationales.eli10: If push-in pressure falls while inside pressure is high, brain flow drops.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A stroke causes weakness and visual-spatial neglect but not aphasia. Which pattern is most likely?

rationales.whyCorrect: Right-hemisphere injury commonly impairs spatial attention and left-sided motor function.
rationales.eli10: The right brain map and opposite-side movement pathways are affected.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How does excitotoxicity enlarge ischemic brain injury?

options.text: Excess glutamate drives calcium entry and enzyme damage

rationales.whyCorrect: Energy failure causes glutamate accumulation, receptor activation, and toxic calcium influx.
rationales.eli10: A stuck-on message floods cells with calcium and harmful activity.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does diffuse axonal injury occur with rapid rotational trauma?

options.text: Shearing strains tear connections across brain regions

rationales.whyCorrect: Different tissue densities rotate at different speeds and stretch axons.
rationales.eli10: A sudden twist pulls delicate brain wires apart.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which difference separates delirium from typical Alzheimer progression?

options.text: Delirium is acute and fluctuating, while Alzheimer decline is gradual

rationales.whyCorrect: Time course and fluctuating attention distinguish acute brain dysfunction from chronic neurodegeneration.
rationales.eli10: One is a sudden flickering light; the other dims slowly.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can Parkinson's disease cause both movement and nonmovement symptoms?

options.text: Neurodegeneration involves interconnected motor and nonmotor circuits
Only the spinal cord is involved

rationales.whyCorrect: Degeneration and transmitter imbalance extend beyond a single motor pathway.
rationales.eli10: The damaged network connects movement with mood, sleep, and other jobs.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What causes type 1 diabetes mellitus?

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells

rationales.whyCorrect: Beta-cell destruction produces an absolute insulin deficiency.
rationales.eli10: The body's guards mistakenly destroy its insulin makers.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is central to type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Insulin resistance with progressive beta-cell dysfunction
Autoimmune loss of every beta cell at onset

rationales.whyCorrect: Body tissues respond poorly to insulin, and secretion may later become inadequate.
rationales.eli10: The insulin key works poorly, and the key factory may tire.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is hypoglycemia?

rationales.whyCorrect: Hypoglycemia deprives the brain and other tissues of readily available glucose.
rationales.eli10: There is too little sugar fuel in the blood.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is hyperthyroidism?

rationales.whyCorrect: High thyroid activity accelerates metabolic processes.
rationales.eli10: The body's speed-setting hormone is turned too high.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is peptic ulcer disease?

options.text: A break in stomach or duodenal mucosa

rationales.whyCorrect: Ulcers occur when mucosal defenses are overcome by acid-peptic injury.
rationales.eli10: The protective lining develops a sore.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What defines cirrhosis?

options.text: Diffuse liver fibrosis with regenerative nodules

rationales.whyCorrect: Chronic liver injury reorganizes tissue into scar and nodules.
rationales.eli10: The liver becomes a stiff, lumpy scarred filter.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is pancreatitis?

options.text: Inflammation caused by pancreatic enzyme-related injury

rationales.whyCorrect: Premature enzyme activation can digest pancreatic tissue and trigger inflammation.
rationales.eli10: Digestive chemicals activate too early and hurt their own factory.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which disorders are inflammatory bowel diseases?

rationales.whyCorrect: These chronic immune-mediated disorders inflame different regions and layers of bowel.
rationales.eli10: The immune system keeps inflaming parts of the intestine.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is malabsorption?

options.text: Impaired uptake of nutrients from the intestine
